linux.description: Fundamental commands for moving through the filesystem and checking machine identity.

commands.description: Print working directory path
commands.flagExplanation: Outputs the absolute path of the current directory

commands.description: List all directory entries including hidden files with long details
commands.flagExplanation: -l enables long listing (permissions, owner, size, timestamp); -a displays hidden files beginning with .

commands.description: Print complete system and kernel architecture information
commands.flagExplanation: Crucial during enumeration to identify Linux kernel version for vulnerability matching

commands.description: Display Linux distribution release details and version
commands.flagExplanation: Shows whether host is Ubuntu, Debian, RedHat, CentOS, or Alpine

commands.description: Print current username, UID, primary GID, and supplemental groups
commands.flagExplanation: Verifies whether current shell belongs to root, www-data, or a standard user

linux.description: Managing POSIX permissions, ownership, and special SUID bits.

commands.description: Change file access permissions
commands.flagExplanation: 600 grants owner read/write only (essential for SSH keys); 755 grants owner rwx and others r-x

commands.description: Change file owner and group
commands.flagExplanation: -R applies ownership recursively across all subdirectories and files

commands.description: Locate files with SUID bit set across the entire system
commands.flagExplanation: SUID binaries execute with file owner privileges (often root), a primary vector for privilege escalation

commands.description: List allowed sudo commands for the current user
commands.flagExplanation: Inspects /etc/sudoers to see if current user can run binaries as root without password (NOPASSWD)

linux.description: Rapid extraction of indicators, credentials, and error patterns from logs.

commands.description: Recursively search files for sensitive secrets or credentials
commands.flagExplanation: -r recursive, -n prints line numbers, -i ignores case, -E enables extended regex

commands.description: Stream authentication attempts and sudo executions in real time
commands.flagExplanation: -f follows log file changes dynamically as events occur; use /var/log/secure on RHEL/CentOS

commands.command: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -10
commands.description: Extract the top 10 most frequent client IP addresses from an Apache or NGINX access log
commands.flagExplanation: awk extracts first column (IP), sort arranges, uniq -c counts duplicates, sort -nr sorts numerically descending

linux.description: Inspecting running processes, daemons, and system resources.

commands.description: Snapshot of every running process on the system
commands.flagExplanation: a displays all users, u displays user-oriented format with CPU/MEM %, x displays processes without terminal

commands.description: Check operational state and recent logs of a systemd unit
commands.flagExplanation: Shows if service is active, enabled on boot, PID, and recent journal entries

commands.description: Inspect detailed systemd execution logs for a specific service
commands.flagExplanation: -x adds explanatory help, -e jumps to end of log, -u filters by unit name

commands.description: Forcefully terminate an unkillable or rogue process
commands.flagExplanation: Signal 9 immediately drops process without cleanup

linux.description: Diagnosing active connections, listening sockets, and DNS resolution.

commands.description: Display all listening TCP and UDP sockets with owning process PID and name
commands.flagExplanation: -t TCP, -u UDP, -l listening only, -p process info (requires sudo), -n numeric ports

commands.description: Display all network interfaces, IP addresses, and routing tables
commands.flagExplanation: Modern replacement for deprecated ifconfig and route commands

commands.description: Inspect HTTP headers and TLS handshake details without downloading payload
commands.flagExplanation: -I sends HEAD request, -v enables verbose mode showing SSL certificate and negotiation

commands.description: Query DNS records for a domain name
commands.flagExplanation: +short outputs concise answers; +trace follows delegation from root servers

ports.description: Transfers files between client and server. Control channel runs on port 21.
ports.securityImplication: Sends credentials and data in unencrypted plaintext. Highly vulnerable to packet sniffing and anonymous login misconfigurations.

ports.description: Encrypted remote terminal management and secure file transfer.
ports.securityImplication: Frequent target of automated password brute-force bots. Recommended to enforce public key authentication, disable root login, and rate-limit with Fail2ban.

ports.description: Legacy unencrypted command-line interface.
ports.securityImplication: Entire session including passwords transmitted in cleartext. Deprecated everywhere in production; replace immediately with SSH.

ports.description: Server-to-server email routing and delivery.
ports.securityImplication: Open mail relays can be hijacked to send spam. Modern secure mail submission uses port 587 with STARTTLS.

ports.description: Resolves domain names to IP addresses. UDP 53 handles standard queries; TCP 53 handles zone transfers and responses > 512 bytes.
ports.securityImplication: Vulnerable to DNS amplification DDoS, cache poisoning, and DNS tunneling for data exfiltration.

ports.description: Dynamically assigns IP addresses to client hosts on local subnets.
ports.securityImplication: Rogue DHCP servers can distribute malicious default gateway IPs or DNS servers to perform MITM attacks.

ports.description: Simplified file transfer without authentication, used for network booting (PXE) and router configuration backups.
ports.securityImplication: Zero authentication mechanism. Anyone with network access can download or overwrite files if not firewalled.

ports.description: Unencrypted World Wide Web traffic.
ports.securityImplication: All web traffic, cookies, and login credentials can be snooped or altered by in-path network devices. Always redirect to HTTPS (port 443).

ports.description: Ticket-based network authentication protocol used by Microsoft Active Directory.
ports.securityImplication: Target of Kerberoasting (requesting TGS tickets and cracking service account password hashes offline) and AS-REP roasting.

ports.description: Legacy client email retrieval.
ports.securityImplication: Sends usernames and passwords in cleartext. Use POP3S on port 995 with SSL/TLS instead.

ports.description: Synchronizes system clocks across computer systems over variable latency data networks.
ports.securityImplication: Historically abused in massive UDP reflection/amplification DDoS attacks (monlist command).

ports.description: Assigns dynamic ports for Microsoft Windows Remote Procedure Call services.
ports.securityImplication: Assists attackers in enumerating running Windows services and Active Directory domain controllers. Never expose to public internet.

ports.description: Legacy Windows file and printer sharing over NetBIOS.
ports.securityImplication: Provides unauthenticated null session enumeration of Windows users, shares, and policies.

ports.description: Retrieves and manages email messages directly on the mail server.
ports.securityImplication: Unencrypted authentication. Must be replaced with IMAPS (port 993) using TLS.

ports.description: Monitors network-attached devices for conditions requiring administrative attention.
ports.securityImplication: SNMP v1 and v2c use cleartext 'community strings' (often default 'public' or 'private') that reveal complete network topologies. Require SNMPv3 with encryption.

ports.description: Directory services querying for users, computers, and groups across networks.
ports.securityImplication: Transmits queries and directory credentials in cleartext if not protected by LDAPS (port 636) or StartTLS.

ports.description: Encrypted web communications protecting privacy and integrity between browser and server.
ports.securityImplication: Inspect certificate expiration, deprecated cipher suites (TLS 1.0/1.1), and web application vulnerabilities (SQLi, XSS) operating inside the encrypted channel.

ports.description: Native Windows file, printer, and IPC sharing directly over TCP/IP.
ports.securityImplication: Critical target for lateral movement, Pass-the-Hash, and historical wormable exploits (EternalBlue / MS17-010, WannaCry). Never expose to the public internet.

ports.description: Secure encrypted email submission directly over a TLS-wrapped connection.
ports.securityImplication: Requires validated TLS certificates; protects outgoing email against eavesdropping.

ports.description: Standard modern port for mail client submission with opportunistic TLS encryption.
ports.securityImplication: Vulnerable to STRIPTLS downgrade attacks if the mail client does not strictly enforce TLS encryption.

ports.description: Encrypted directory service access preventing credential sniffing across the enterprise.
ports.securityImplication: Enforce LDAPS channel binding and signing on Windows Domain Controllers to prevent relay attacks.

ports.description: Secure, encrypted email retrieval keeping user credentials and message bodies private.
ports.securityImplication: Industry standard for desktop and mobile email clients.

ports.description: Encrypted POP3 email retrieval.
ports.securityImplication: Protects legacy POP3 mail clients against credential interception.

ports.description: Relational database server listening port.
ports.securityImplication: Frequent target for SA account brute-force and xp_cmdshell command execution for full host compromise.

ports.description: Listens for incoming client database connections to Oracle instances.
ports.securityImplication: Default SID enumeration (TNS listener) and brute-force attacks if left accessible across untrusted network zones.

ports.description: Default port for MySQL and MariaDB relational databases.
ports.securityImplication: Never bind to 0.0.0.0 publicly without firewall restrictions and mutual TLS authentication.

ports.description: Microsoft proprietary graphical remote desktop access protocol.
ports.securityImplication: One of the number one initial access vectors in enterprise ransomware attacks when exposed without MFA or VPN.

ports.description: Default port for PostgreSQL open-source object-relational database.
ports.securityImplication: Audit pg_hba.conf to ensure only authorized application subnets can initiate connections.

ports.description: Graphical desktop sharing system across platforms.
ports.securityImplication: VNC passwords are limited to 8 characters and often unencrypted. Must be tunneled through SSH or VPN.

ports.description: In-memory key-value cache and message broker.
ports.securityImplication: By default lacks authentication and binds to all interfaces. Attackers routinely overwrite SSH authorized_keys or crontabs via Redis config commands.

ports.description: Widely used for development web servers, Tomcat, Jenkins, and HTTP proxy listeners (Burp Suite).
ports.securityImplication: Frequently hosts unauthenticated management dashboards and internal microservices.

ports.description: Common secondary port for secure administrative web consoles and management panels.
ports.securityImplication: Ensure production self-signed certificates are replaced and management access is restricted by IP whitelist.
